comparison: Both strongly support VTA axon ramping-to-reward behavior. OpenEval cites 88.9% quantitative support across multiple analyses (C4-C6, C37, C53, C55, C79), while peer reviewers explicitly affirm the finding as 'solid' with 'thorough' and 'rigorous' analysis. High agreement on this core finding.

Both support LC encoding of kinematic variables rather than spatial position. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative evidence for velocity and motion onset encoding (C5, C7, C38-C39, C54, C56-C57, C70, C78, C80), while peer reviewers accept LC axons 'ramped up before initiation of movement' and 'correlated invariantly with velocity.' Strong concordance.

Both support velocity encoding in VTA and LC populations. OpenEval notes quantitative differences and acknowledges small VTA sample size (C40-C41, C62, C65-C67), while peer reviewers affirm 'activity of both VTA axons and LC axons increased with the mice's running speed' with 'thorough' analysis. Agreement on finding despite sample size concerns.

Both support LC novelty response with sustained activity. OpenEval documents 90s/6 lap duration and prevalence (36/87 ROIs, C8-C9, C42-C43, C82-C85, C88, C90-C93, C124), while peer reviewers explicitly affirm 'dramatic increase in activity lasting 90s' as 'solid evidence' with 'rigorous' analysis. Strong agreement.

Both express uncertainty about VTA novelty response due to severe underpowering. OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN noting single responsive axon insufficient (C86-C87, C111-C112), while peer reviewers raise 'significant concern' about 'severely underpowered' recordings from 'mere 7 axons' and note potential false negative. Strong concordance on limitation.

Both support reward removal experiment dissociating reward from behavioral signals. OpenEval emphasizes differential VTA vs LC effects (C58-C61, C68-C69, C74-C75, C106-C108), while peer reviewers confirm 'diminished ramping activity in VTA DA axons, but no changes in the LC axons' as validating reward-locked activity. Strong agreement.

Both support two-component model of LC novelty response. OpenEval describes sophisticated dissection with running vs immobile analyses (C94-C102), while peer reviewers initially requested this analysis and subsequently accepted findings showing 'increased (but transient) signal in LC axons...during periods of immobility.' Agreement after revision.

Both support LC response to familiar environment onset as additional control. OpenEval notes shorter duration (20s vs 90s) supports arousal interpretation (C103-C104), while peer reviewers accept data but question whether 'LC input to dHC signals novelty still valid' given this finding. Agreement on data, mild divergence on interpretation scope.

Both strongly support main conclusions of functional dissociation. OpenEval affirms VTA reward encoding and LC novelty/kinematic encoding are well-supported (C10-C11, C141-C143, C147-C148), while peer reviewers provide 'convincing evidence' of 'partly distinct environmental, behavioral and cognitive factors' as 'important findings.' Strong concordance on primary conclusions.

Both support VTA velocity encoding as genuine heterogeneity independent of reward. OpenEval notes persistence across conditions and comparison to soma recordings (C109-C110, C67), while peer reviewers accept interpretation without challenge, noting 'methodological rigor.' Agreement on heterogeneity interpretation.

Divergent evaluations of sample size adequacy. OpenEval supports methodology with 'appropriate' sample sizes and anatomical verification (C44-C52), while peer reviewers express 'significant concerns' about 'severely underpowered' VTA recordings (7 vs 87 LC axons) and note lack of predefined target sample sizes. Major disagreement on methodological rigor.

Divergent evaluations of calcium indicator methodology. OpenEval supports use of Cre-driver lines with citations as 'appropriate genetic tools' (C44-C47), while peer reviewer raises concern that pooling data from 'different calcium indicators with differential kinetics' (GCaMP6S and GCaMP7b) makes it 'very challenging to draw any valid conclusions.' Significant methodological disagreement.

OpenEval supports background/rationale claims about catecholaminergic modulation and traditional VTA/LC views (C1-C3, C12-C18) as appropriately cited. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these introductory contextual claims.

OpenEval supports comprehensive literature review on VTA and LC functions in hippocampus (C19-C34) as well-cited and establishing rationale for comparative approach. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.
OpenEval supports motivation for axon-level recordings based on heterogeneity literature (C35-C36). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this methodological justification.

OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN speculative interpretations about LC effects on place cell excitability and plasticity (C115-C119), noting these remain hypotheses requiring direct testing. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific speculative claims.

OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN speculative claims about novelty mechanisms (C120-C128), noting these are reasonable but untested hypotheses requiring functional manipulations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific mechanistic speculations.

OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN speculative claims about instant place fields (C129-C135), noting temporal correlation is suggestive but requires causal testing. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific speculative interpretations.

OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN speculative hypothesis about activity-dependent neurotransmitter switching (C136-C137, C139-C140), noting this remains entirely speculative without direct measurements. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this mechanistic proposal.

OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN arousal interpretation and attention effects (C144-C146), noting this is reasonable given behavioral correlates but would benefit from direct arousal measurements or causal manipulations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific interpretive claims.

OpenEval supports methodological transparency regarding sex limitation with justification (C149-C151), though notes generalizability limitation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific methodological details.
